lead: This year the Fortieth Friday, Nalpatham Velli, meets the feast of St Joseph. The readings belong to the Friday, and they stand at the door of the Week of the Passion. Abraham looks out at the smoke of Sodom, and we learn that God remembered his prayer and brought Lot out. Israel nearly goes to war over an altar by the Jordan, and sends envoys first. Paul asks Christians to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed them, and names the root of Jesse, the royal line in which Joseph, son of David, gave Jesus his place. At Bethany Jesus calls a dead man out of the tomb, days before his own burial. The key words are remember, one altar, welcome and come out. Over all of them stands the quiet man who guarded the Lord’s childhood, whose prayers the Church seeks for the grace of a good death.

set: This short passage follows the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. In chapter 18 Abraham stood before the Lord and pleaded for the city, bringing the number of the righteous down from fifty to ten (18:22–33). In chapter 19 not even ten are found, and Lot and his family are led out by the two messengers. Now Abraham, who has heard nothing since, comes back in the morning to the place of his prayer.
str: v. 27: Abraham returns early to the place where he prayed.
v. 28: what he sees: smoke rising.
v. 29: the narrator’s explanation: God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out.
v. 30: Lot, afraid to stay in Zoar, goes to live in a cave.
¶ The reading stops at the cave and does not go on to the sad story of Lot’s family that follows. It wants us to stay with v. 29.
kw: In the Bible God’s remembering is never a mere recollection. It leads to action. “God remembered Noah” and the waters went down (8:1); he remembered Rachel, and she conceived (30:22); he remembered his covenant, and the Exodus began (Exodus 2:24).
Kiln or furnace. The same word describes the smoke on Sinai (Exodus 19:18). The fire that destroys and the fire of God’s presence look alike from a distance.
The word for God’s overturning of Sodom. Words from the same root became a standing phrase for divine judgment in the prophets (Amos 4:11; Isaiah 13:19).
vv: Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the Lord;
He goes back to where he prayed, without knowing the answer. Prayer here includes the courage to come back and look.
God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow,

Notice the wording: the rescue of Lot is credited to the memory of Abraham’s prayer. Abraham had asked for the city and was given his nephew. He saw only smoke. The reader knows what he did not know: his prayer was heard, in a way he could not see.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham’s heart is attuned to the Lord’s compassion and that he dares to intercede for others with bold confidence (CCC 2571); intercession belongs to a heart in tune with God’s mercy (CCC 2635). For anyone praying for a child or a spouse far from God, this verse is a comfort: we do not always see what our prayer has done.

set: Two and a half tribes (Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh) had received land east of the Jordan on condition that they fight beside the others (Numbers 32). They kept their word (Joshua 1:12–18) and have just been sent home with a blessing (22:1–9). On the way they build a huge altar near the river. The law asks for one place of worship (Deuteronomy 12:5–14), and the tabernacle now stands at Shiloh (18:1). To the western tribes the new altar looks like a breakaway.
str: vv. 10–11: the altar, and the report.
v. 12: the assembly gathers at Shiloh for war.
vv. 13–15: Phinehas and ten chiefs are sent.
vv. 16–18: the charge, recalling the sin at Peor.
v. 19: a generous offer: come and share our land.
v. 20: the warning from Achan.

¶ The reading stops before the answer. In vv. 21–29 the eastern tribes explain that the altar is no place of sacrifice. It is a witness for their children that they too belong to the Lord. War is avoided (vv. 30–34).
kw: A strong word for unfaithfulness to God, used in vv. 16 and 20, and of Achan (7:1). The fear is not about a building but about a whole people drifting away.
Used repeatedly in vv. 16–19. The envoys see a rebellion, and they see the danger to everyone: the sin of one group brings harm on “the whole congregation” (v. 18).
The priest whose zeal at Peor stopped a plague (Numbers 25:7–13). The priest best known for zeal is the one sent, and he comes to talk.
vv: the whole assembly of the Israelites gathered at Shiloh, to make war against them.
Their anger comes from a real love of God’s law. Good zeal can still act on a wrong reading of the facts.
Then the Israelites sent the priest Phinehas son of Eleazar
This is the turning point. Before anyone draws a sword, someone goes to ask. The Great Fast may ask the same of our families and parishes.
take for yourselves a possession among us;
Under the anger there is real generosity. If your land seems unclean, come and live with us. They would rather give up some of their own land than lose their brothers.
Did not Achan son of Zerah break faith in the matter of the devoted things,
Sin is never wholly private in the Bible. It wounds the whole body.
ch: St Paul says, “there is one body” (Ephesians 4:4) and calls Christ “our peace” who broke down the dividing wall (Ephesians 2:14). St Ignatius of Antioch urges Christians to keep one Eucharist, for there is one flesh of the Lord, one cup and one altar, as there is one bishop (To the Philadelphians 4; in substance). The Catechism speaks of the altar of the New Covenant as the Lord’s Cross, from which the sacraments flow (CCC 1182), and of the wounds to the Church’s unity as something we must pray and work to heal (CCC 817–822).

set: Paul writes to Rome around AD 57. Chapters 14–15 deal with a real tension in the community between the “strong” and the “weak” over food and days. Many scholars think this tension ran largely, though not wholly, between believers of Gentile and of Jewish background. This passage rounds off the discussion, and with it the main body of the letter. Christ himself is the model, and Scripture is the proof.
str: v. 7: the command: welcome one another, as Christ welcomed you.
vv. 8–9a: Christ served the Jews for God’s faithfulness, and the Gentiles for God’s mercy.
vv. 9b–12: four quotations from Scripture.
v. 13: a blessing of hope.

¶ The quotations are from Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1 and Isaiah 11:10. So the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms all give the same witness: the nations will praise God together with his people.
kw: To take someone to oneself, as into a home or friendship. The same verb opens the discussion (14:1).
A remarkable title for Christ. He came as a servant to his own Jewish people, to confirm God’s promises to them (compare Matthew 15:24). God’s word to Israel stands.

From Isaiah 11. The POC has “a shoot from Jesse”. Jesse was David’s father, and the title means the Messiah of the royal house. “The one who rises” (ho anistamenos) may also suggest to Paul’s readers the Resurrection.
vv: Welcome one another, therefore, just as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
The measure of our welcome is the welcome we received: while we were sinners (5:8). The goal is God’s glory, which shines when people who differ sit at one table.
Christ has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of the truth of God
“Truth” here includes God’s faithfulness to his promises. Because God keeps faith with Israel, the Gentile believer can trust him as well.
The root of Jesse shall come,

Today this line turns our minds to St Joseph. Matthew and Luke trace Jesus’ legal descent through Joseph, “son of David” (Matthew 1:20). The Catechism says that God called him so that Jesus should be born into the messianic lineage of David (CCC 437).
May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
Paul’s title for God is unusual and beautiful. Hope is the last word of the main body of the letter, and it is above all a gift of the Spirit.
ch: The Catechism defines hope as the virtue by which we desire the kingdom and eternal life, relying on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). The Second Vatican Council adds that the Church awaits the day, known to God alone, when all peoples will address the Lord with one voice (Nostra Aetate 4). On St Joseph’s day it is fitting to remember that Christian hope reached its goal through a family, and that God’s promises to Israel came through the patient obedience of one man of David’s house.

set: This is the last and greatest of the signs in John’s Gospel before the Passion. Lazarus of Bethany has died, and Jesus delayed his coming on purpose (11:6, 15). He has told Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25), and he has wept (11:35). Bethany is near Jerusalem (11:18). This sign leads the council to plan his death (11:47–53), so the giving of life to Lazarus will cost Jesus his own.
str: vv. 38–39: at the tomb: “Take away the stone”, and Martha’s objection.
v. 40: “you would see the glory of God”.
vv. 41–42: Jesus’ prayer of thanks to the Father.
vv. 43–44: the call, and Lazarus comes out still bound.
v. 45: many believe.
kw: A strong word (vv. 33, 38), used elsewhere of a stern warning or an indignant snort. Jesus is deeply moved: with grief, and many think with anger at death itself. The POC has “sighing”, which is gentler than the Greek.
The goal of the whole sign (11:4, 40). In John the glory of God is seen in Jesus’ works and above all on the Cross (12:23–24).

Lazarus comes out bound in grave cloths and will need them again one day. On Easter morning the wrappings of Jesus are left behind in the tomb, and the same word for the face cloth is used (20:6–7). He rises never to die again.
vv: Jesus said, “Take away the stone.”

Jesus could move the stone himself. He asks people to do what they can. The objection comes from a woman of faith, and it is honest: “already there is a stench”. A later Jewish tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days. The four days make plain that Lazarus is truly dead.
Father, I thank you for having heard me.

He gives thanks before anything has happened. The Catechism notes that thanksgiving comes first here, and that the Father always hears his Son (CCC 2604). He prays aloud so that the crowd may know that he comes from the Father (v. 42).
When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”

It is a call by name, as the shepherd calls his own (10:3), and it fulfils his own word about the dead hearing his voice (5:28–29). John uses the same strong verb for the shouts at the entry into Jerusalem (12:13) and before Pilate (19:6). Here it is Jesus who cries out, and the cry gives life.
Unbind him, and let him go.
He gives life, and asks others to do the rest. St Augustine sees here the ministry of the Church, which looses the penitent whom Christ has called to life (in substance).
Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what Jesus did, believed in him.

All the people in this scene are Jews: Jesus, Martha, Mary, Lazarus, and the mourners who came to comfort the sisters. Many believe. When John goes on to speak of opposition, he means certain authorities (11:47), not the people as a whole.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person (CCC 994), and that the raising of Lazarus was a return to ordinary earthly life, unlike Christ’s Resurrection, which passes beyond death (CCC 646). St Augustine reads the four days as a soul long buried in the habit of sin, and he finds hope for such a soul in Christ’s loud cry (in substance). So a sinner who feels too long in the tomb can hear this Gospel as his own.

qa: Abraham prayed for Sodom and it was still destroyed. Did his prayer fail?

Not ten righteous people were found, so the city fell. And yet “God remembered Abraham” and rescued Lot. Abraham’s prayer did more than he could see. God’s answer to our prayer is often larger or different than what we can see from where we stand.
Why does the Church honour St Joseph so greatly, when Scripture gives him no spoken word?

Because of what he was given to do. He was the husband of Mary and, in the place of a father, guarded and raised the Son of God. Matthew calls him “a righteous man” (Matthew 1:19). Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church in 1870, and St John Paul II wrote about him in Redemptoris Custos (1989), as Pope Francis did in Patris Corde (2020). In the Gospels he speaks by what he does. The Church also entrusts the dying to him as patron of a happy death (CCC 1014).
Lazarus died again. So what was the point?

The sign points beyond itself. It shows that Jesus has power over death, and that those who believe in him will live even though they die (11:25–26). Lazarus returned to this life. Christ opens the way to a life where death has no more power (CCC 646).
rite: Nalpatham Velli marks the completing of the first stage of the Great Fast and the turn toward the Passion of the Lord. In many Syro-Malabar parishes the Way of the Cross is made with special devotion, and some climb a hill shrine on foot. Where the feast of St Joseph is kept today, many places also hold the meal for the poor (oottu) in honour of the Holy Family. How fast and feast are kept together on this day follows the direction of one’s own eparchy. It is a fitting meeting. The man who took the Child and his Mother and rose in the night to obey is the patron of families and of the dying. As Lazarus is called out of the tomb, we may ask St Joseph to walk with us through the coming days, and to stay with us at the hour of our own death.
study: Abraham went back to the place of prayer without knowing the answer. For whom do I keep praying while seeing only smoke?
The tribes sent Phinehas to talk before they went to war. What quarrel in my family or parish needs someone to go and ask first?
“Welcome one another.” Whom do I find hard to welcome in my own Church, and how has Christ welcomed me?
Jesus asked others to unbind Lazarus. Who around me has come back to faith but is still bound, and needs my help? What can I learn from St Joseph’s quiet way of serving?
